content.text: Students synthesize the unit’s key ideas by showing how Katherine’s persistence connects learning, data, and teamwork in Chapter 17.
Scientific discovery grows through questions, evidence, and collaboration. Making hidden stories visible helps us understand who gets included in science and why it matters.
Students will read Chapter 18 and continue tracing how Katherine’s work becomes more visible and more essential.
Students need to explain how an innovator’s actions and evidence-based work made a difference, not just retell events.

Unit 3 Lesson 15 Student Edition
3-Column Chart graphic organizer
Develop an explanatory paragraph with relevant details from Chapter 17 to explain how Katherine Goble’s persistence in lectures and editorial meetings advanced understanding of spaceflight.
Use nominalizations, clear pronouns, and cause/effect transitions to connect curiosity, determination, and collaboration in analytical writing.

Turn and Talk
Language Study
Modeled Writing
Quick Write
Turn and Talk
Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the following question.
How does Katherine’s curiosity, persistence, and collaboration help to make her whole team stronger?
Language Study
“Katherine’s persistence in the lecture series led to deeper participation in editorial meetings, and her questions helped the team strengthen its understanding of spaceflight.”
Directions:

In this lesson, we study how writers explain and make connections between ideas using precise language. Instead of listing events, analytical writing names concepts like persistence and participation and shows how one idea leads to another.
Read the sentence with a partner. Discuss how the sentence is constructed and how it helps to explain the connection between Katherine’s “persistence” and her team’s understanding of spaceflight.
What action has been turned into an abstract idea in this sentence?
Why might a writer use
persistence
instead of saying Katherine kept going?
Which words show a cause-and-effect relationship?
What does “led to” connect in the sentence?
What does the word “her” refer to?
What does the word “its” refer to?
How does the sentence show collaboration?
To write analytically, we:
turn actions into abstract nouns (persist → persistence)
use clear pronouns so the reader knows who or what is being discussed
connect ideas using cause-and-effect language like “led to”
This helps writing explain ideas, not just list events.
Read the basic version of the sentence and revise it so it sounds more analytical:
Katherine participated in meetings. She helped the team understand spaceflight better.
Use one abstract noun and one clear pronoun.
Part A: Connecting Ideas
Evidence Collection
Directions:

Reread three key moments in Chapter 17: the section where Katherine keeps attending the lecture series, the section where she participates in editorial meetings, and the section where her learning helps the team understand spaceflight more deeply. Use the 3-Column Chart to paraphrase details, not copy full sentences. In the final column, explain how each detail connects to one or more of these ideas: curiosity, determination, and collaboration.
Label each column as indicated:
Column 1: Key Moment
Column 2: Paraphrased Detail
Column 3: How the Detail Connects to the Big Ideas
Part B: Drafting the Explanation
Modeled Writing
Directions:
Use your 3-Column Chart and draft a five-to-six-sentence explanatory paragraph in your Journal that responds to the prompt:
Write a paragraph explaining how Katherine’s curiosity, determination, and collaboration contribute to Langley’s understanding of spaceflight. Use details from the text to support your response.
Checklist
As you draft, check your work for these four things:
Did I answer the whole question in my first sentence?
Did I use at least two Chapter 17 details?
Did I connect the ideas instead of explaining them separately?
Did I use clear pronouns and academic words like
persistence
participation
, or
collaboration
Quick Write
Directions:
In three to four sentences, explain how connecting ideas can make explanatory writing more effective.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the following question.
Ask:
How does Katherine’s curiosity, persistence, and collaboration help to make her whole team stronger?

When someone keeps learning, asking questions, and encouraging others, it helps a team work together and solve challenging problems. In Chapter 17, Katherine’s persistence and drive carry over to her team, making them even more effective.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
We have discussed some big ideas in Chapter 17 and next we will learn how to turn our ideas into a clearly written academic explanation.
Activate prior learning from Lesson 14 and connect the unit’s essential question to today’s writing task.
Students will learn how analytical writers move from listing events to explaining ideas by using nominalization, clear pronoun reference, and cause-and-effect language.
Language Study
Display and read aloud this revised mentor sentence based on the Chapter 17 section, where Katherine keeps attending the lecture series and the editorial meetings:
“Katherine’s persistence in the lecture series led to deeper participation in editorial meetings, and her questions helped the team strengthen its understanding of spaceflight.”
Teach: Moving from Events to Analysis
Say these Directions:

In this lesson, we study how writers explain and make connections between ideas using precise language. Instead of listing events, analytical writing names concepts like persistence and participation and shows how one idea leads to another.
Read the sentence with a partner. Discuss how the sentence is constructed and how it helps to explain the connection between Katherine’s “persistence” and her team’s understanding of spaceflight.
Model and Deconstruct
Ask:
What action has been turned into an abstract idea in this sentence?
persistence
Ask:
Why might a writer use
persistence
instead of saying Katherine kept going?
It sounds more formal and explains the idea behind the action.
Ask:
Which words show a cause-and-effect relationship?
“led to”
Ask:
What does “led to” connect in the sentence?
her persistence and her participation in meetings
Ask:
What does the word “her” refer to?
Katherine
Ask:
What does the word “its” refer to?
the team
Ask:
How does the sentence show collaboration?
It explains that her questions helped the team.
Say:
To write analytically, we:
turn actions into abstract nouns (persist → persistence)
use clear pronouns so the reader knows who or what is being discussed
connect ideas using cause-and-effect language like “led to”
This helps writing explain ideas, not just list events.
Say:
Read the basic version of the sentence and revise it so it sounds more analytical:
Katherine participated in meetings. She helped the team understand spaceflight better.
Use one abstract noun and one clear pronoun.
Katherine’s participation in the meetings helped the team deepen its understanding of spaceflight.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that we have practiced using some sentence tools that help to connect details to ideas, we can apply them to our explanatory writing.
Support students in using nominalizations, pronouns, and transitions to build precise analytical sentences.
Language Focus:
Nominalization
Subjective, objective, and possessive pronouns
Cause/effect transitions
Point out that nominalization helps students explain abstract ideas without writing run-on sentences.
If students overuse she without a clear noun, prompt them to reread and identify exactly who each pronoun names.
“You said ‘she kept trying’—we can say: ‘Her persistence continued even when she was not originally included.’”
“You said ‘it helped them’—we can say: ‘Her participation helped the team deepen its understanding of the science.’”
“Katherine’s ___ led to ___.”
“Through her participation, she contributed to ___.”
“Her ___ helped the team ___.”
Invite students to compare how abstract ideas are named in English and in a home language, especially if a noun form is more common in one language than the other.
If students create run-ons while combining ideas → Prompt: “Stop after your first big idea. Now add a transition like ‘led to’ or ‘as a result’ before the next part.”
If students use unclear pronouns like she or it several times in a row → Prompt: “Replace one pronoun with the exact noun so the reader knows who or what you mean.”
Students correctly transform a verb into a noun form to raise academic tone.
Students use pronouns that clearly refer back to Katherine or the team.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Nominalization
Offer a verbal prompt with word pairs students can choose from: persist/persistence, participate/participation, collaborate/collaboration.
Struggling with: Pronoun Clarity
Have students underline the noun first, then draw an arrow to the pronoun that replaces it.
Ready for extension

Ask students to revise their sentence again using both a nominalization and a cause/effect connector such as “as a result” or “which led to.” Challenge students to add a second clause that explains how the action affected Langley’s understanding of spaceflight.
Teach students how nominalization, pronoun clarity, and transitions help them explain abstract ideas with stronger academic tone.
Part A: Connecting Ideas (W.6.9.b) (12 minutes)
Students reread Chapter 17 with a clear purpose: to gather evidence that connects Katherine’s persistence to curiosity, determination, and collaboration.
Evidence Collection
Say these Directions:

Reread three key moments in Chapter 17: the section where Katherine keeps attending the lecture series, the section where she participates in editorial meetings, and the section where her learning helps the team understand spaceflight more deeply. Use the 3-Column Chart to paraphrase details, not copy full sentences. In the final column, explain how each detail connects to one or more of these ideas: curiosity, determination, and collaboration.
Label each column as indicated:
Column 1: Key moment
Column 2: Paraphrased Detail
Column 3: How the Detail Connects to the Big Ideas
Teach:
Say:
I do not want to collect random details that all say the same thing. Instead, I want evidence that connects, like a chain.
First, I look for a detail that shows Katherine wanting to know more than what was required, because that shows curiosity.
Next, I look for a detail that shows her fighting for her right to learn, because that demonstrates her determination.
Then, I look for a detail that shows her sharing her knowledge with others, because that shows collaboration.

When I organize the evidence this way, I can explain how the ideas work together. This is stronger than writing three separate sentences that never connect. My paragraph will sound clear and authoritative because each piece of evidence has a job.
Display a completed sample row if students need support:
Key moment
Paraphrased Detail
How the Detail Connects to the Big Ideas
In the section where Katherine keeps attending the lecture series
She keeps learning the science behind the calculations instead of stopping with her assigned task.
This shows curiosity because she asks questions to gain a deeper understanding of scientific concepts.
In the section where her work helps the team think more clearly about spaceflight
Her persistence leads to stronger explanations and better shared understanding within the team.
This shows determination because Katherine keeps pushing forward to learn more and solve problems, even when it is difficult.
In the section where she joins editorial meetings
She brings what she learns into a shared discussion with other experts.
This shows collaboration because she shares what she learns with others so they can be a stronger team.
Support students in paraphrasing evidence and linking each detail to an abstract idea.
Language Focus:
Paraphrasing
Evidence-to-idea explanation
Multi-part analytical frames
Before Evidence Collection (preparation step—optional)
Students whisper-read one text landmark and orally complete the frame “This detail shows ___ because ___.”
Prompt students to keep the evidence brief and the explanation fuller; many students will over-copy text and under-explain.
When students label a detail with only one idea, ask whether that detail also connects to another idea in the chain.
“You said ‘she learned more’—we can explain that by saying ‘her curiosity led to deeper scientific understanding.’”
“That idea connects to evidence because what she learned made the team’s reasoning stronger.”
“This detail shows curiosity because Katherine ___.”
“This moment becomes evidence when ___.”
“Through her participation in ___, she contributed to collaboration by ___.”
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk to clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language, if helpful, before sharing with the whole group.
If students copy long sections from the text → Prompt: “Say the detail in your own words using no more than ten words first, then add your explanation.”
If students explain each big idea separately without showing connection → Prompt: “Add one phrase that links the ideas, such as ‘which allowed’ or ‘as a result.’”
Students paraphrase a specific Chapter 17 detail accurately.
Students explain how one detail connects to more than one abstract idea.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Choosing Evidence
Narrow the rereading task to one landmark first and ask, ‘What did Katherine do here, and what changed because of it?”::
Struggling with: Paraphrasing
Let students orally rehearse a paraphrase with a partner before writing it into the chart.
Struggling with: Written Output
Allow students to provide an oral recording of one evidence explanation or use speech-to-text tools before transferring it to the organizer.
Ready for extension
Ask students to star one detail that connects to all three ideas and explain why it is the strongest piece of evidence.
Invite students to add a fourth note explaining how Katherine’s persistence challenged assumptions about who belongs in scientific conversations.
Part B: Drafting the Explanation (W.6.2) (18 minutes)
Modeled Writing

This part of the lesson guides students in turning evidence from Chapter 17 into a focused explanatory paragraph. Students learn to begin with a clear, overarching idea, select two purposeful details, and connect those details in a logical chain that shows how Katherine’s curiosity, determination, and collaboration contribute to Langley’s understanding of spaceflight.
Teach:
Say:

I need my first sentence to answer the whole question, not just name one event. If I start with “Katherine went to meetings,” the reader still does not know why that matters. Instead, I begin with an idea that connects everything: Katherine’s determination helped Langley deepen its understanding of spaceflight. Then I choose one lecture detail to show how curiosity becomes knowledge, and one meeting detail to show how that knowledge is shared through collaboration. Before finishing, I reread to make sure my sentences form one clear chain of ideas rather than three separate facts.
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance:

Katherine Goble’s persistence helped Langley deepen its understanding of spaceflight because she refused to stop learning at the edge of her assigned role. In the section where she keeps attending the lecture series, her curiosity pushes her to understand the science behind the calculations more fully. That deeper learning is shared when she participates in editorial meetings with other experts. Through her participation, she does not just gather information for herself; she contributes to collaboration by bringing questions and knowledge into a shared scientific discussion. As a result, the Langley team’s broader understanding grows stronger because of how Katherine connects curiosity, learning, and teamwork. Her persistence matters because it turns her private effort into public scientific progress.
Say these Directions:
Use your 3-Column Chart and draft a five-to-six-sentence explanatory paragraph in your Journal that responds to the prompt:
Write a paragraph explaining how Katherine’s curiosity, determination, and collaboration contribute to Langley’s understanding of spaceflight. Use details from the text to support your response.
Checklist (W.6.2)
As you draft, check your work for these four things:
Did I answer the whole question in my first sentence?
Did I use at least two Chapter 17 details?
Did I connect the ideas instead of explaining them separately?
Did I use clear pronouns and academic words like
persistence
participation
, or
collaboration
Support students in producing clear analytical writing that connects multiple abstract ideas in one cohesive paragraph.
Language Focus:
Cohesion through pronouns and transitions
Analytical explanation
Academic register
Before Drafting (preparation step—optional)
Students orally rehearse their topic sentence using one nominalization before they begin writing.
Confer first with students whose drafts list curiosity, evidence, and collaboration separately; prompt them to add a linking phrase that shows sequence or cause.
Watch for pronoun ambiguity, especially repeated uses of
she, it,
or
they
without a clear noun nearby.
“You said ‘she learned more and then she helped’—we can say: ‘Her growing understanding became evidence she could share with the team.’”
“That idea connects to collaboration because participation in meetings allowed knowledge to be tested and shared.”
“Katherine’s persistence led her to ___, which allowed ___.”
“Through her participation in ___, she contributed to ___.”
“As a result, Langley’s understanding of spaceflight became ___ because ___.”
Encourage students to rehearse a sentence aloud before writing so they can hear whether the pronoun reference and transitions make sense.

If students write one long run-on sentence to hold all three ideas → Prompt: “Break after your first cause-and-effect idea, then begin the next sentence with ‘Through her participation’ or ‘As a result.’”
If students use pronouns that could refer to Katherine or the team → Prompt: “Replace one pronoun with the exact noun and reread the paragraph for clarity.”
Students use at least one nominalization to raise academic tone.
Students connect two or more details in a logical chain rather than summarizing each detail separately.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Starting The Paragraph
Offer this opening frame: “Katherine’s persistence helped Langley understand spaceflight better because ___.”
Struggling with: Connecting Ideas
Ask students to draw arrows between evidence notes before drafting so they can see the chain from curiosity to evidence to collaboration.
Struggling with: Written Output
Allow students to dictate their first draft to a partner or use speech-to-text tools and then revise for pronoun clarity and transitions.
Ready for extension
Challenge students to include one sentence explaining why Katherine’s participation also changed who could be seen as an expert.
Invite students to revise one sentence for stronger academic tone by replacing a verb phrase with a nominalization.
Criterion
1 – Developing
2 – Approaching
3 – Meets
W.6.2.b — Student develops the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
Writing includes few or no relevant facts, definitions, details, or examples.
Writing includes some relevant information, but development is uneven or partially explained.
Writing develops the topic with clear, relevant facts, definitions, details, quotations, or examples that support understanding.
W.6.2.c — Student uses appropriate transitions to clarify relationships among ideas and concepts.
Writing uses few or no transitions, making relationships unclear.
Writing uses some transitions, but connections between ideas may be uneven or partially clear.
Writing uses appropriate transitions that clearly show relationships among ideas and concepts.
Lesson 15 Writing Rubric: Explanatory Paragraph — Katherine's Curiosity & Determination

Writing prompt: Write a paragraph explaining how Katherine Johnson's curiosity, determination, and collaboration contributed to her success at NASA. Use evidence from Hidden Figures and precise academic language.
Criteria
1 — Beginning
2 — Developing
3 — Proficient
Precise Language & Style
Domain Vocabulary & Tone
Language is vague or informal. No domain vocabulary connected to mathematics, space exploration, or Katherine's work is used. Tone is not academic.
Some precise language and domain vocabulary is used, but word choices are inconsistent. The tone is generally formal but shifts to informal phrasing in places.

Precise language and domain vocabulary — curiosity, determination, collaboration, trajectory, calculation, segregation — is used accurately throughout. The tone is consistently formal and academic, appropriate for explaining Katherine's contribution.
Part A: Collecting the Chain of Ideas (W.6.9.b)
Students will gather and organize evidence showing how Katherine Goble’s persistence connects curiosity, evidence, and collaboration.
Part B: Drafting the Explanation (W.6.2.d)
Students will write a cohesive explanatory paragraph using precise language and evidence from Chapter 17.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
In three to four sentences, explain how connecting ideas can make explanatory writing more effective.

Connecting ideas makes explanatory writing more effective because it helps the reader see how the information fits together. When ideas are linked, the paragraph feels like one clear explanation instead of a list of separate facts. It also shows the writer’s thinking by explaining why the details matter. As a result, the reader can understand the bigger point the writer is trying to make.
Support students in reflecting on which language choices helped them produce clearer analytical writing.
Language Focus:
Metalinguistic reflection
Explanation of strategy use
Precise reference to language choices
Prompt students to name a specific writing move rather than saying the paragraph was better.
Encourage students to connect a language choice to its effect on the reader.
“You said ‘I used better words’—we can say: ‘I used nominalization to make my explanation sound more analytical.’”
“That idea connects to cohesion because clear pronouns helped the reader follow who was doing the work.”
“One writing move that helped me was ___ because ___.”
“My paragraph became clearer when I used ___.”
“A phrase that helped me connect ideas was ___.”
Allow students a brief turn-and-talk to rehearse the name of one writing move before they write independently.
If students give only a general reflection → Prompt: “Name the exact word, phrase, or transition that helped your writing.”
If students focus only on effort instead of language use → Prompt: “What sentence move made your explanation easier to follow?”
Students identify a specific language tool they used.
Students explain how that tool improved clarity, cohesion, or academic tone.
Students will reflect on how connecting ideas can make explanatory writing more effective.
